Question: Let \(A,\) \(M,\) and \(C\) be nonnegative integers such that \(A + M + C = 12.\) What is the maximum value of \[ \begin{aligned} &A \cdot M \cdot C + A \cdot M \\ &\quad {}+ M \cdot C + C \cdot A? \end{aligned} \]
Solution:
The expression is symmetric in the three variables. To see whether making two variables closer together helps, write
\[
F(A,M,C)=(C+1)AM+C(A+M).
\]
If \(C\) and \(A+M\) stay fixed, only the product \(AM\) can change.

There are finitely many allowed triples, since each variable is an integer between \(0\) and \(12\), so a maximum exists. Suppose two variables at a maximum differ by at least \(2\). By symmetry, call the larger one \(A\) and the smaller one \(M\), so \(A\ge M+2\). Replace them by \(A-1\) and \(M+1\). The new variables remain nonnegative integers with the same total, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
&F(A-1,M+1,C)-F(A,M,C)\\
&\quad=(C+1)\bigl((A-1)(M+1)-AM\bigr)\\
&\quad=(C+1)(A-M-1)>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This contradicts maximality. Thus no two variables at a maximum can differ by \(2\) or more.

Their average is \(4\). Any integer triple with this average other than \((4,4,4)\) has one entry at least \(5\) and another at most \(3\). Therefore the maximum occurs at \(A=M=C=4\), where
\[
F=4^3+3\cdot4^2=64+48=\boxed{112}.
\]
The answer is choice E.
